tasks.title: Leonardo da Vinci's Mechanical Knight
tasks.instruction: Listen to a talk in an art history class. Then answer the questions.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the lecture?

options.A: To review Leonardo da Vinci's most famous artistic works
options.B: To explain how early machines led to modern robotics
options.C: To highlight a lesser-known achievement of Leonardo da Vinci
options.D: To describe technological advances during the Renaissance

questions.stem: Why does the speaker mention Leonardo's fascination with the human body?

options.A: To indicate his contributions to medical science
options.B: To point out a key influence on Leonardo's designs
options.C: To explain why he spent more time studying anatomy than engineering
options.D: To emphasize Leonardo's artistic skills

questions.stem: What does the speaker suggest about Leonardo's mechanical understanding?

options.A: It depended on help from other scientists.
options.B: It was shown only in his sketches.
options.C: It was advanced for his time.
options.D: It relied mainly on trial and error.

questions.stem: What attitude does the speaker express toward the reconstruction of "Leonardo's Robot"?

options.A: He is relieved that some design flaws were corrected.
options.B: He is happy that Leonardo's sketches were published.
options.C: He is doubtful of the artistic value of the robot.
options.D: He is impressed by what the robot could do.

tasks.title: Lewis Latimer: Inventor and Innovator
tasks.instruction: Listen to a talk on a history podcast. Then answer the questions.

questions.stem: What does the speaker say is a false belief about nineteenth-century inventors?

options.A: That their inventions were available to the general public
options.B: That they were famous in their time
options.C: That they worked in laboratories
options.D: That they created their inventions alone

questions.stem: How did Lewis Latimer learn to be a drafter?

options.A: By teaching himself
options.B: By studying with a tutor
options.C: By receiving help from an inventor
options.D: By going to a special school

questions.stem: Why does the speaker mention that Latimer was a poet?

options.A: To point out why Hiram Maxim was impressed by Latimer at first
options.B: To help explain the beauty of Latimer's technical drawings
options.C: To introduce Latimer's collaborative project with a musician
options.D: To describe how Latimer's career changed after he worked as a drafter

questions.stem: What did Latimer achieve in his work with Hiram Maxim?

options.A: Latimer helped make lightbulbs more available to the public.
options.B: Latimer invented a new way of producing electricity.
options.C: Latimer created a new drawing style that was useful for inventors.
options.D: Latimer made a drawing that helped convince the public of the usefulness of electric lighting.

tasks.title: Kinetic Art: Motion and Visual Storytelling
tasks.instruction: Listen to a talk on an art podcast. Then answer the questions.

questions.stem: What is the main topic of the talk?

options.A: The technical challenges faced by certain artists
options.B: The development and significance of a particular type of art
options.C: The influence of traditional art forms on modern artists
options.D: The popularity of kinetic art among contemporary patrons

questions.stem: According to the talk, what role did the Hungarian artist László Moholy-Nagy play in the development of kinetic art?

options.A: He criticized the use of technology in art.
options.B: He advanced the idea of using movement and light in art.
options.C: He was the first to use air and wind to manipulate art.
options.D: He established the first kinetic art museum.

questions.stem: What challenge is associated with kinetic art, as mentioned in the talk?

options.A: It requires video monitors.
options.B: It can make it difficult for the audience to engage.
options.C: It can involve technical difficulties.
options.D: It is rarely displayed in major galleries.

questions.stem: Why does the speaker describe kinetic art as "a multisensory experience"?

options.A: To summarize the way kinetic art engages its viewers
options.B: To emphasize that kinetic art is hard to understand
options.C: To highlight an advantage of using video in kinetic art
options.D: To explain the technical requirements of kinetic art installations

tasks.title: Renaissance Tapestries
tasks.instruction: Listen to a talk in an art history class. Then answer the questions.

questions.stem: Why does the speaker mention Renaissance paintings and sculptures?

options.A: To contrast them with a less well-known art form from the same period
options.B: To provide examples of collaborative art forms
options.C: To highlight the religious nature of Renaissance art
options.D: To assert their superiority over other forms of Renaissance art

questions.stem: According to the talk, what was a key advantage of tapestries over frescoes?

options.A: They were cheaper to produce.
options.B: They could be displayed in museums.
options.C: They were easier to transport.
options.D: They depicted more complex scenes.

questions.stem: According to the speaker, what sometimes happened to tapestries while being transported from one location to another?

options.A: They were used as insulation.
options.B: They were stolen.
options.C: They became damaged.
options.D: Their designs were copied by other artists.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the process of tapestry creation during the Renaissance?

options.A: It required fewer resources than other art forms.
options.B: It involved a collaborative effort among several artisans.
options.C: It was mainly practiced in religious settings.
options.D: It was more popular than painting.

options.A: They increase soil nutrients.
options.B: They can lead to soil erosion.
options.C: They are a solution to desertification.
options.D: They reduce the need for reforestation.

options.A: To explain its role in accelerating desertification
options.B: To discuss its impact on agricultural productivity
options.C: To highlight the benefits of rising temperatures
options.D: To describe changes in biodiversity

tasks.title: Soil Casts and Ancient Agriculture
tasks.instruction: Listen to a talk in an archaeology class. Then answer the questions.

questions.stem: What is the main focus of the talk?

options.A: Ways in which ancient peoples supplied nitrogen and moisture to their fields
options.B: Similarities between gardens of ancient Rome and Central America
options.C: A method for studying planting practices of ancient cultures
options.D: An example of how modern agriculture can learn to benefit from ancient knowledge

questions.stem: Why do researchers inject plaster into soil?

options.A: To make the soil more stable
options.B: To protect plant roots in the soil
options.C: To replicate an ancient practice that existed in different parts of the world
options.D: To obtain casts that match decayed material in shape

questions.stem: What does the speaker say is a main feature of the agricultural system practiced in the Maya village in Central America?

options.A: It takes advantage of plants that do not decay quickly.
options.B: It combines a variety of crops that support each other's growth.
options.C: It relies on a complex irrigation system.
options.D: It changes crops from year to year.

questions.stem: What does the speaker imply about Roman garden designers?

options.A: They tried to replicate nature.
options.B: They considered roses to be more beautiful than other flowers.
options.C: They valued both beauty and practicality.
options.D: They were interested in foreign plant species.

tasks.title: Infant Language Learning and the Wug Test
tasks.instruction: Listen to a talk in a linguistics class. Then answer the questions.

questions.stem: What does the Wug Test show about young children?

options.A: They can come up with new words.
options.B: Drawings can help them learn language.
options.C: They can remember new words for a long time.
options.D: They understand grammatical rules.

questions.stem: What does the speaker emphasize about spoken language?

options.A: It is easier to learn than written language.
options.B: It has some highly complex syllables.
options.C: It differs significantly between adults and children.
options.D: It does not clearly mark word boundaries.

questions.stem: What did the head-turn preference experiment indicate about babies?

options.A: They are very good at recognizing patterns.
options.B: They learn short words before learning longer words.
options.C: They understand some words by the time they are eight months old.
options.D: They benefit from pauses when working to understand language.

questions.stem: What will the speaker discuss next?

options.A: Ways to learn language effectively
options.B: Ways to improve attention and memory
options.C: Statistical information about different languages
options.D: Research on the connection between language learning and other mental skills

tasks.title: Keystone Species and Yellowstone Wolves
tasks.instruction: Listen to a talk in a science podcast. Then answer the questions.

questions.stem: Why does the speaker talk about arches in architecture?

options.A: To point out a similarity to rock arches in nature
options.B: To help illustrate an important concept
options.C: To argue against a common comparison
options.D: To show a difference between life science and technology fields

questions.stem: According to the talk, what is a keystone species?

options.A: A species that is necessary to maintain balance in an ecosystem
options.B: A species that has no predators within an ecosystem
options.C: A species that is too numerous for a healthy ecosystem
options.D: A species that is negatively affected by environmental changes

questions.stem: In the early 20th century, what happened to the wolves in Yellowstone National Park?

options.A: Their population increased dramatically when their prey population increased.
options.B: They became a government-protected species.
options.C: They were eliminated over farming and safety concerns.
options.D: Their population decreased significantly because of disease.

questions.stem: How did an increasing elk population affect the Yellowstone ecosystem?

options.A: Many species were negatively affected due to the elks' diet.
options.B: Various animals that prey on elk were attracted to the area.
options.C: Some areas developed an overgrowth of plants while others had too little vegetation.
options.D: The population and range of the wolves also increased.

tasks.title: The Precautionary Principle
tasks.instruction: Listen to a talk in an environmental science class. Then answer the questions.

questions.stem: What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: A method for gathering data to inform decision-making models
options.B: A guideline for making certain kinds of policy decisions
options.C: The unintended consequences of conservation projects
options.D: The importance of research in planning sensitive projects

questions.stem: What does the speaker say was the main concern with the proposed road project in Tanzania?

options.A: Increased tourism traffic and pollution
options.B: Uncertainty surrounding the project's funding
options.C: The possibility of disrupting animal migrations
options.D: Opposition from local communities because of land disputes

questions.stem: According to the speaker, what does the precautionary principle emphasize?

options.C: Avoiding anything that risks serious harm even when the harm is not certain

options.C: To explain differences between several types of ecosystems
options.D: To discuss new research into microorganisms found in soil

questions.stem: What does the speaker point out about extracellular polymeric substances?

options.A: They hold soil particles together.
options.B: They indicate that soil is degraded.
options.C: They are an important nutrient source for microbes.
options.D: They can replace chemical fertilizers under certain conditions.

questions.stem: What is a reference site in the work that the speaker describes?

options.A: A laboratory where microbes are grown.
options.B: A location where restoration efforts have previously failed.
options.C: A degraded area that is used for testing interventions.
options.D: A healthy ecosystem used as a model.

questions.stem: What does the professor say about the California vineyard before the intervention?

options.A: Its soil contained high numbers of bacteria.
options.B: Its vines were infected with harmful fungi.
options.C: It was surrounded by forested land.
